title: Ratatouille confit byaldi
subtitle: Tian-style slow-roasted Provençal vegetables
excerpt: Thin rounds of courgette, tomato, onion, and pepper arranged in overlapping circles over a piperade base, drizzled with olive oil and slow-roasted until soft and almost jammy. The elegant, tian-style interpretation of ratatouille.
sourceNotes: Confit byaldi is a Provençal preparation related to ratatouille. The name 'byaldi' connects it to the Turkish dish 'İmam bayıldı' (stuffed aubergine), and the overlapping tian presentation is associated with the cooking of Provence. The dish is documented in Thomas Keller's The French Laundry Cookbook (1999) and in earlier French regional references. The technique of slow-confiting vegetables in olive oil over a piperade base appears in multiple Provençal cooking texts. This version uses the classical Provençal method.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be made the day before and served at room temperature or gently reheated. The flavour improves overnight.
recipe.temperatureNote: low and slow for the confiting stage

glossaryTerms.definition: A Basque sauce or base made from softened onions, peppers, and tomatoes cooked down in olive oil. Used here as the base layer under the vegetables.

A Provençal dish in which sliced vegetables are arranged in overlapping layers in a baking dish and slow-roasted in olive oil. Also the name of the shallow terracotta dish traditionally used to cook it.

content.text: Heat 3 tablespoons of the olive oil in a large, wide pan over medium heat. Add the finely chopped onion and diced peppers and cook for 15 minutes, stirring regularly, until very soft. Add the chopped garlic and cook for 2 minutes. Add the tinned tomatoes, crush them down with a spoon, and season. Cook for 15 minutes until the mixture is thick and almost dry. Scatter in half the thyme leaves.
Heat the oven to 150°C (fan 130°C). Spread the piperade evenly across the base of a large, shallow baking dish.

Arrange the courgette, tomato, and onion rounds on top of the piperade in overlapping concentric circles or rows, alternating the three vegetables. Tuck the sliced garlic and remaining thyme sprigs between the rounds. Drizzle with the remaining 3 tablespoons of olive oil and season generously with salt and pepper.

Cover the dish tightly with foil and bake for 1 hour. Uncover and continue baking for another hour until the top layer is soft, slightly caramelised at the edges, and the vegetables have collapsed down into the piperade. Leave to rest for 20 minutes before serving.

items.symptom: Vegetable rounds are still firm after 2 hours
items.cause: Oven temperature too low, or foil seal not tight enough
items.fix: Ensure the foil is tight. Add another 20 to 30 minutes covered, then uncover for the last 20 minutes to get colour on top.
Next time use plum tomatoes, which are drier. This time, carefully pour off excess liquid and cook uncovered a little longer.

content.text: This presentation of ratatouille is closely associated with Provence and the Côte d'Azur. It is a summer dish that makes the most of courgettes and tomatoes at their seasonal peak. The dish is as good at room temperature as it is hot, which suits summer entertaining well, since not everything can come out of the oven at the same moment. It is served alongside grilled fish, roasted lamb, or simply with good bread and a bottle of rosé.
